title: Unrolling implementation
text:
Unrolling implementation
Unrolling methods directly train encoder, decoder and dynamic in one time using a constrained structure : \[
\min_{A, \mathcal E, \mathcal D} ||x_{t+\Delta_t} - \mathcal D(e^{A \Delta_t}\mathcal E({x_t}))||_2^2
\]

Reflexion on the dynamic :
In “pure” koopman method, the dynamic would be independent for each eigenfunction and live in complex space, in most deep learniing implemented method \(A\) is a dense matrix.
If we wanted to restric the dynamic we have two options :

1. Restrict \(A\) to be tri-diagonal + antisymmetric :
As \((a + b i)(\alpha + \beta i) = a \alpha - b \beta   + (b \alpha + a \beta)i\), if we represent our eigenfunctions as \(\begin{bmatrix} a & b \end{bmatrix}^T\) with the second coordinate being the complex one and the first one being the real one, we could represent the multiplcation with \(\begin{bmatrix}\alpha &-\beta \\ \beta&\alpha\end{bmatrix}\). Stacking all the eigenfunctions together we end up having a large block-diagonal matrix we can exponentiate.
Then we have : \[
\dot z = (\gamma I + \beta J)z \text{ with } J = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \to z(t) = e^{(\gamma I + \beta J)t}z_0 = e^{\gamma t} \begin{bmatrix} \cos \beta t & -\sin \beta t \\ \sin \beta t & co \beta t \end{bmatrix}
\] Then, as shown in the complex example we can just linearly compose the complex and imaginary part of the dynamic to have a projection (taking in account the presence of the conjugate eigenfunction).
Pros : we have a generic form between the dense and restricted form, it’s easy to implement
Cons : I am not sure how optimized is the exponential of tridiagonal matrix in pytorch
A = Blockdiage(alpha, beta) # Params to learn (alpha & beta : (J), (J)) -> (J, 2, 2)
psi = encoder(x) # (B, J, 2) - complex and real are separated
eA = expm(A*t, dim=-1) # (Exponential of 2x2 matrix is actually a closed form with sin/cos)

tilde_psi_next = einsum(eA, psi, 'j k l, n j l -> n j k') # (B, J, 2)
tilde_x_next = decoder(tilde_psi_next)  # (B, P)
L = ||tilde_x_next - x_next|||  # (B,)


2. Polar representation :
As shown in the complex notebook, we can do the evolution quickly if we represent the eigenfunctions in polar form an learn the magnitude and angle of the eigenvalues. \[
|\psi(t)| = e^{\gamma t} r(0) \quad \angle \psi(t) =  \omega t + \angle \psi(0)
\] And then to do the decoding (at least in linear way) you need to come back to complex notation (from the polar form) which is standard but requires to compute the cos and sin of the polar form.
Something interesting is that we can ask the encoder to directly predict the polar form which is an interesting asset to avoid the complex to polar transformation.
Restriction on parameter and outputs : For parameter \(\gamma \in \R\) and \(\omega \in \R\) so we are good. For the encoder output, at first sight it looks like \(|\psi(t)| \in \R^+\) and \(\angle \psi(t) \in [0; 2\pi]\) but in practice polartocomplex deals with negative absolute value and angles of any value so we don’t really have constraints.
Pros : simple representation in the latent space, no matrix representation required
Cons : not a generic form with the dense representation, requires the non-linear transformation at decoding time,
gamma, omega = random() # Params to learn (gamma & omega : (J), (J))
psi = encoder(x) # (B, J, 2) - complex and real are separated
tilde_psi_next = psi[..., 0]*exp(gamma*t), psi[..., 1]+omega*t # (B, J, 2) 
tilde_psi_next_complex = polartocomplex(tilde_psi_next) # (B, J, 2) 
tilde_x_next = decoder(tilde_psi_next)  # (B, P)
L = ||tilde_x_next - x_next|||  # (B,)
Globally we can have this view of koopman autoencoder that unite the two perspectives :

This view is more tighted with the first code the exponential is done of \(L \times L\) matrices, in the case where \(L=2\) the fact to have a close form is an advantage.
Q : If you express \(A = \gamma I + \omega J\) we have \(e^{At} =e^{\gamma I t} + e^{\omega J t}\) do we have an easy to compute for \(e^{\omega J t}\) knowing it’s anti-symmetric and no diagonal.
Q : What is the exact link between those approaches and SSL models like mamba
Q : Globally we could generalize the idea we represent here into taking a complex dynamic, break it into a set of \(J\) “simple” dynamics with fewer interaction (involving the interaction of \(L\) variables) in a way you can recover the dynamic after, for me it would mean that we could think about non-linear dynamic in the different groups. What do you think ?

title: The function difference trick — an exact linearisation between two points
text:
Let’s say we have a function \(D : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^n\), continuously differentiable, and we want to compute
\[
D(\tilde z) - D(z)
\]
Then we can setup a function :
\[
\gamma(s) = z + s \, \delta z \implies \gamma'(s) = \delta z
\]
Where \(\delta z = \tilde z - z\)
and \(g(s) = D(\gamma(s))\)
Thus \(g'(s) = J_D(\gamma(s))\gamma'(s)\) and \(g(s=1) = D(\tilde z)\), \(g(s=0) = D(z)\).
We can write :
\[
D(\tilde z) - D(z) = \int_{s=0}^{s=1} J_D(z + s \, \delta z ) \, \delta z \, ds = \underbrace{\left[\int_{s=0}^{s=1} J_D(z + s \, \delta z ) \, ds\right]}_{\bar A(z, \tilde z)} \delta z
\]
The bracket is the whole point. It is a matrix — the Jacobian averaged along the segment joining \(z\) to \(\tilde z\) — and it satisfies
\[
D(\tilde z) - D(z) = \bar A(z, \tilde z) \, \delta z
\]
exactly, for any \(\delta z\), however large. This is not a first-order approximation. \(\bar A\) is a secant operator: unlike the tangent \(J_D(z)\), it depends on both endpoints.

title: The function difference trick — an exact linearisation between two points
section: 2.1 How fast does the estimate converge?
text:
2.1 How fast does the estimate converge?
We compare the estimate \(\bar A \, \delta z\) against the true difference \(D(z + \delta z) - D(z)\), averaged over 10 random pairs, as a function of the number of Jacobian evaluations.


Code
def mean_rel_error(rule, N, pairs):
    errs = []
    for z, dz in pairs:
        s, w = rule(N)
        true = D(z + dz) - D(z)
        errs.append((estimate_difference(z, dz, s, w) - true).norm() / true.norm())
    return torch.stack(errs).mean().item()


pairs = [(torch.randn(n), torch.randn(n)) for _ in range(10)]

          for name, rule in rules}

for i, N in enumerate(Ns):

for rule_name, _ in rules:
    ax.loglog(Ns, np.clip(curves[rule_name], 1e-17, None), marker="o", label=rule_name)
ax.loglog(Ns, 0.3 / np.sqrt(Ns), "k--", lw=1, label=r"$1/\sqrt{N}$")

Figure 2: Mean relative error of the estimated difference. Monte-carlo tracks the \(1/\sqrt{N}\) reference; gauss-legendre reaches machine precision with ~32 nodes.





The identity is confirmed: gauss-legendre drives the error to machine precision (~\(10^{-15}\)) with about 32 Jacobian evaluations, and is already at \(10^{-11}\) with 16. The net is smooth, so the quadrature converges spectrally.
Monte-carlo is the loser, and by a wide margin. It sits on the \(1/\sqrt N\) line: 256 evaluations to still be around 3%, where midpoint is already near \(10^{-6}\) and gauss-legendre is at machine precision. It is also visibly noisy — the error is not even monotone in \(N\). For a one-dimensional integral, sampling is the wrong instinct; keep it only if you need the unbiasedness.

2.2 Exact, not first-order
This is what \(\bar A\) buys over the tangent \(J_D(z)\). We fix a direction and grow \(\|\delta z\|\):


Code
z = torch.randn(n)
direction = torch.randn(n)
direction /= direction.norm()
s, w = nodes_gauss_legendre(64)

print(f"{'||dz||':>8} {'path integral':>16} {'tangent J(z) dz':>18}")
for scale in [0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0]:
    dz = scale * direction
    true = D(z + dz) - D(z)
    e_path = (estimate_difference(z, dz, s, w) - true).norm() / true.norm()
    e_tan = (jacrev(D)(z) @ dz - true).norm() / true.norm()
    print(f"{scale:8.2f} {e_path:16.1e} {e_tan:18.1e}")

The tangent linearisation degrades exactly as expected, its error growing with the step size until it is meaningless. The path integral stays at machine precision no matter how far apart the two points are — which is the entire content of the trick.

title: Koopman Complex-Valued Eigenfunctions
text:
This is a follow-up to Koopman Eigenfunctions — An Introduction. There we kept things simple by working with real-valued eigenfunctions, but in general the Koopman eigenfunctions \(\kpsi_j\), weights \(\kv_j\) and eigenvalues \(\klam_j\) are complex, even when the observable \(\kg\) itself stays real. This note works through why that’s the case, what it costs computationally, and when it actually matters.
In the introduction we wrote
\[
\begin{aligned}
x &\in \mathbb{R}^p \\
\kg &: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R} \quad \text{(observation function)} \\
\kg(x) &= \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \kv_j \kpsi_j(x)
\end{aligned}
\]
Where
\[
\begin{aligned}
\kpsi_j(T(x_0, t)) &= e^{\klam_j t}\kpsi_j(x_0)
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(\kv_j\) are the weights in the decomposition, \(\kpsi_j\) are the eigenfunctions of the dynamic and \(\klam_j\) their associated eigenvalues.

title: Koopman Complex-Valued Eigenfunctions
section: Question 1: can the eigenspace be complex?
text:
Question 1: can the eigenspace be complex?
In practice it would mean \(\kpsi_j: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{C}\), \(\kv_j \in \mathbb{C}\), \(\klam_j \in \mathbb{C}\).
At first sight it can seem surprising as \(\kg(x) \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(\kg(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \kv_j \kpsi_j(x)\), summing complex numbers is going to return a complex number.
But if the dynamic in Koopman space were operating on real numbers only, it would restrict the ability to represent oscillations, for instance.

Response
Actually, Koopman eigenfunctions can be complex. The idea is that they always come in conjugate pairs \((\kpsi_j, \overline{\kpsi_j})\), and for any real observable \(\kg\) the corresponding coefficients must themselves be complex conjugates of each other, in this way:
\[
\kg(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \kv_j \kpsi_j(x) = \sum_{\text{pairs}\ j} \left( \kv_j \kpsi_j(x) + \overline{\kv_j}\, \overline{\kpsi_j(x)} \right) = 2 \sum_{\text{pairs}\ j} \mathrm{Re}\big(\kv_j \kpsi_j(x)\big)
\]
where the last two sums run over one representative of each conjugate pair (an eigenfunction with a real eigenvalue can be taken real and enters the sum directly, without the factor 2). Thus \(\kg(x)\) stays real while the \(\kpsi_j\) themselves are complex.






NoteProposition



Let \(\kpsi_j\) be a Koopman eigenfunction of \(T\) with eigenvalue \(\klam_j \in \mathbb{C}\). Then \(\overline{\kpsi_j}\) is also a Koopman eigenfunction of \(T\), with eigenvalue \(\overline{\klam_j}\).






TipProof





Let \(\kpsi_k \triangleq \overline{\kpsi_j}\), i.e. \(\kpsi_k(x) = \overline{\kpsi_j(x)} \; \forall x\), and write \(x_t = T(x_0, t)\). Thus:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\kpsi_k(x_t) &= \overline{\kpsi_j(x_t)}\\
&= \overline{e^{\klam_j t}\kpsi_j(x_0)}\\
&= e^{\overline{\klam_j} t}\, \overline{\kpsi_j(x_0)}\\
&= e^{\overline{\klam_j} t}\, \kpsi_k(x_0) \quad \forall x_0, t
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(\kpsi_k\) satisfies the eigenfunction relation with eigenvalue \(\overline{\klam_j}\).

title: Koopman Complex-Valued Eigenfunctions
section: Question 2: if we keep only the \(\mathrm{Re}(\kpsi_j(x))\) do we still need to do integration on complex numbers?
text:
Question 2: if we keep only the \(\mathrm{Re}(\kpsi_j(x))\) do we still need to do integration on complex numbers?
Yes, because the imaginary parts of \(\klam_j\) and \(\kpsi_j(x_0)\) are going to impact \(\mathrm{Re}(\kpsi_j(x))\). Writing \(\klam_j = \gamma + \omega i\):
\[
e^{\klam_j t}\,\kpsi_j(x) = e^{(\gamma+\omega i)t}\big(a_j(x)+ib_j(x)\big) = e^{(\gamma+\omega i)t}\, r_j(x)\, e^{i\varphi_j(x)}
\]
with \(r_j(x) = \sqrt{a_j(x)^2 + b_j(x)^2}\) and \(\varphi_j(x) = \operatorname{atan2}\big(b_j(x),\, a_j(x)\big)\)
Thus:
\[
e^{\klam_j t}\,\kpsi_j(x) = r_j(x)\, e^{\gamma t + i(\omega t + \varphi_j(x))}
= r_j(x)\, e^{\gamma t}\Big(\cos(\omega t+\varphi_j(x)) + i\sin(\omega t+\varphi_j(x))\Big)
\]
Thus \(\mathrm{Re}(e^{\klam_j t}\,\kpsi_j(x)) = r_j(x)\, e^{\gamma t}\cos(\omega t+\varphi_j(x))\), we can see the real part is impacted by \(\omega\) and \(b_j\) (the imaginary parts of the eigenvalue and initial condition).

title: Koopman Complex-Valued Eigenfunctions
section: Question 3: for what kind of dynamic do we need complex eigenfunctions?
text:
Question 3: for what kind of dynamic do we need complex eigenfunctions?
If we take a simple dynamic like:
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = Ax
\]
With \(x \in \mathbb{R}^p\) and \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}\), we can show that \(\kpsi_j(x) = l_j \cdot x\) are Koopman eigenfunctions, where \(l_j A = \klam_j l_j\) are the left eigenvectors of \(A\):
\[
\kpsi_j(T(x_0, t)) = \kpsi_j(e^{At}x_0) = l_j \cdot e^{At} x_0 = e^{\klam_j t}\, l_j \cdot x_0 = e^{\klam_j t} \kpsi_j(x_0)
\]
using \(l_j\, e^{At} = e^{\klam_j t}\, l_j\), which follows from applying \(l_j A = \klam_j l_j\) term by term in the series \(e^{At} = \sum_n \frac{(At)^n}{n!}\).
Thus, if some left eigenvectors of \(A\) (and their corresponding eigenvalues) are complex, the resulting eigenfunctions will be complex too.

Example
Take \(A\) to be a pure rotation generator in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), with state \(x = (x_1, x_2)\) (drawn as \((x,y)\) in the board sketch at the end of this post):
\[
\dot{x} = Ax, \qquad A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\omega \\ \omega & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\]
Koopman eigenfunctions:
\(A\) has two complex left eigenvectors, conjugate of each other as expected from the Proposition above:
\[
\begin{aligned}
l_1 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & i \end{bmatrix}, & \klam_1 &= i\omega \\
l_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -i \end{bmatrix} = \overline{l_1}, & \klam_2 &= -i\omega = \overline{\klam_1}
\end{aligned}
\]
giving the two conjugate eigenfunctions:
\[
\kpsi_1(x) = l_1 \cdot x = x_1 + i x_2, \qquad \kpsi_2(x) = l_2 \cdot x = x_1 - i x_2 = \overline{\kpsi_1(x)}
\]
each evolving as a pure phasor:
\[
\kpsi_1(T(x_0,t)) = e^{i\omega t}\kpsi_1(x_0), \qquad \kpsi_2(T(x_0,t)) = e^{-i\omega t}\kpsi_2(x_0)
\]
i.e. \(\kpsi_1\) rotates at rate \(\omega\) and \(\kpsi_2\) at rate \(-\omega\) in \(\mathbb{C}\), while \(x\) itself rotates in the physical plane — reproducing the two circular sketches from the board photo at the end of this post:


Show plotting code

Figure 1: Physical-space trajectory (left) and the two conjugate eigenfunctions \(\psi_1\), \(\psi_2\) as counter-rotating phasors in the complex plane (right).











NoteEigenfunction products form a lattice





Products of eigenfunctions are eigenfunctions too, with summed eigenvalues:
\[
\big(\kpsi_1 \kpsi_2\big)(T(x,t)) = \kpsi_1(T(x,t))\,\kpsi_2(T(x,t)) = e^{(\klam_1+\klam_2) t}\,\kpsi_1(x)\,\kpsi_2(x)
\]
Here \(\klam_1+\klam_2 = 0\), and indeed \(\kpsi_1(x)\kpsi_2(x) = x_1^2+x_2^2 = \lVert x \rVert^2\), the squared radius — a conserved quantity under a pure rotation, consistent with eigenvalue \(0\).



Reconstruction:
Decomposition of the coordinate observables \(\kg_1(x) = x_1\) and \(\kg_2(x) = x_2\) in the \(\{\kpsi_1,\kpsi_2\}\) basis, using \(\kv_2 = \overline{\kv_1}\) each time (per the Proposition above):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\kg_1(x) = x_1 &= \tfrac{1}{2}\kpsi_1(x) + \tfrac{1}{2}\kpsi_2(x) & (\kv_1 = \tfrac12 \text{ real}) \\
\kg_2(x) = x_2 &= -\tfrac{i}{2}\kpsi_1(x) + \tfrac{i}{2}\kpsi_2(x) & (\kv_1 = -\tfrac{i}{2} \text{ purely imaginary})
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Koopman Complex-Valued Eigenfunctions
text:
Conclusion
Koopman eigenfunctions of a dynamic in real space can be complex and it’s important to represent them in that way. In some works a neural network (encoder) is used to represent Koopman eigenfunctions. In deep learning frameworks it is not common for networks to take real-valued inputs and output complex numbers, so one has to be extra careful about that.

title: Koopman unrolling — learning eigenfunctions from data
text:
In the previous tutorials we found Koopman eigenfunctions by hand. Here everything is learned from data: encoder, dynamic and decoder are trained jointly with a single objective:
\[
\min_{A, \mathcal E, \mathcal D} \; \mathbb E_{(t_0, t)} \, \big|\big| x_{t} - \mathcal D\big(e^{A (t - t_0)}\,\mathcal E(x_{t_0})\big)\big|\big|_2^2
\]
Each block matches an object from the introduction:
Two design choices follow: the dynamic and the decoder.

title: Koopman unrolling — learning eigenfunctions from data
text:
3.1 Data and simulation
Same system as the complex example — we know its spectrum analytically:

\(\psi(x) = x_1 + i(x_2 - c\,x_1^2)\), eigenvalue \((\gamma, \omega) = (1, 4)\)
exact linear reconstruction from the lattice: \(\psi^2 \to (2, 8)\) and \(\psi\bar\psi \to (2, 0)\)

So after training we can check whether the optimizer rediscovers this spectrum.


Code
@dataclass
class ComplexPoint:
    a: float
    c: float
    w: float

    def f(self, t, x):
        """x (..., 2) -> dx/dt (..., 2)"""
        x1, x2 = x[..., 0], x[..., 1]
        xp1 = self.a * x1 - self.w * x2 + self.w * self.c * x1**2
        xp2 = (
            self.w * x1
            + self.a * x2
            + self.a * self.c * x1**2
            - 2 * self.c * self.w * x1 * x2
            + 2 * self.c**2 * self.w * x1**3
        )
        return torch.stack([xp1, xp2], dim=-1)

fp = ComplexPoint(1.0, 3.0, 4.0)

text:
3.2 Training
The three blocks assemble into \(\tilde x_t = \mathcal D(e^{A(t - t_0)} \mathcal E(x_{t_0}))\):


Code
class KoopmanModel(nn.Module):
    """
        Encode a reference state, propagate it with the latent dynamic
        up to the requested times, decode back to physical space.
    """
    def __init__(self, encoder, dynamic, decoder):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder, self.dynamic, self.decoder = encoder, dynamic, decoder

    def forward(self, t0, x0, t):
        """
            Params :
                t0 (b)    : reference times
                x0 (b p)  : reference states
                t (b k)   : times we want to predict
            Return :
                x (b k p) : predicted states
        """
        z0 = self.encoder(x0)                   # (b j l)
        z  = self.dynamic.propagate(t0, z0, t)  # (b k j l)
        return self.decoder(z)                  # (b k p)


P, J_MODES, L_DIM = 2, 8, 2

model = KoopmanModel(
    encoder = MLPEncoder(P, J_MODES, L_DIM),
    dynamic = ScalingRotation2D(J_MODES, L_DIM),
    decoder = LinearDecoder(P, J_MODES, L_DIM),
)


Training loop:

each trajectory gets a random reference point \((t_0, x_{t_0})\)
we supervise the prediction at every observed time
negative gaps included — backwards propagation comes for free with the matrix exponential



Code
def unroll_loss(model, x, t_grid):
    """Random reference point per trajectory, predict the whole trajectory."""
    b = x.shape[0]
    i0 = torch.randint(0, x.shape[1], (b,))
    t0, x0 = t_grid[i0], x[torch.arange(b), i0]  # (b), (b p)
    t = repeat(t_grid, 'k -> b k', b=b)          # (b k)
    return F.mse_loss(model(t0, x0, t), x)


opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

    loss = unroll_loss(model, x_train[idx], t_grid)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

    if step % 100 == 0:
        with torch.no_grad():
            val = unroll_loss(model, x_val, t_grid)
        logs['step'].append(step)
        logs['train'].append(loss.item())
        logs['val'].append(val.item())

text:
3.4 Did we recover the spectrum?
Each mode carries a readable eigenvalue \(\lambda_j = \gamma_j + i\,\omega_j\), to compare against the analytic lattice \((1, 4), (2, 8), (2, 0)\). Two details:

the sign of \(\omega_j\) is a conjugacy — we look at \(|\omega_j|\)
unused modes receive no training signal — we weight each mode by its contribution to the reconstruction (usage)



Code
gamma = model.dynamic.gamma.detach()
omega = model.dynamic.omega.detach().abs()

# usage: RMS of each mode's contribution to the reconstruction over val states
with torch.no_grad():
    z  = model.encoder(rearrange(x_val, 'n t p -> (n t) p'))  # (nt, j, l)
    Vb = rearrange(model.decoder.V.weight, 'p (j l) -> j p l', j=J_MODES)
    contrib = es(Vb, z, 'j p l, n j l -> n j p')              # (nt, j, p)
    usage   = contrib.norm(dim=-1).pow(2).mean(0).sqrt()      # (j)

for jj in usage.argsort(descending=True):
    print(f"mode {jj}:  gamma {gamma[jj]: .2f}   |omega| {omega[jj]:.2f}   usage {usage[jj]:.2f}")

NoteHow the usage is computed





The linear decoder splits the reconstruction into per-mode contributions:
\[
\tilde x = V z = \sum_j V_j\, z_j
\qquad\qquad
\text{usage}_j = \sqrt{\;\mathbb E_x\big[\,||V_j\, z_j(x)||_2^2\,\big]\;}
\]

we must measure the product \(V_j z_j\): weights or latents alone are meaningless, the model can rescale one and compensate in the other (\(z_j \to \alpha z_j\), \(V_j \to V_j / \alpha\))
usage \(\approx 0\) means no training signal on \((\gamma_j, \omega_j)\): the mode can sit anywhere on the spectrum plot

title: Koopman unrolling — learning eigenfunctions from data
text:
3.5 Error decomposition
When the forecast is off: is it the representation or the dynamics? The autoencoding path skips the propagation and probes the coders alone:
\[
\bar z(t) = \mathcal E\big(x(t)\big), \qquad \bar x(t) = \mathcal D\big(\bar z(t)\big)
\]
Against the forecast path \(\tilde z(t) = e^{A(t - t_0)}\mathcal E(x(t_0))\), \(\tilde x = \mathcal D(\tilde z)\), the forecast error telescopes exactly:
\[
\underbrace{x - \tilde x}_{\text{forecast error}} \;=\; \underbrace{(x - \bar x)}_{\text{reconstruction error}} \;+\; \underbrace{(\bar x - \tilde x)}_{\text{propagation error}}
\]

reconstruction — can the encoder/decoder pair represent the state at all?
propagation — does the encoded trajectory follow the linear dynamic?

With the linear decoder the propagation term is exact and splits per mode:
\[
\bar x - \tilde x = V(\bar z - \tilde z) = \sum_j V_j\, (\bar z_j - \tilde z_j)
\]
Note: \(\bar x\) is in-distribution — the gap \(t - t_0 = 0\) was supervised as a special case of unrolling.






NoteWhat changes with an MLP decoder





The telescoping identity still holds. But the propagation term is only a first-order map of the latent error,
\[
\bar x - \tilde x = J_{\mathcal D}(\tilde z)\,(\bar z - \tilde z) + \mathcal O\big(||\bar z - \tilde z||^2\big)
\]
and the per-mode split disappears.





Code
with torch.no_grad():
    # forecast path: reference at t0 = 0, propagated to the whole grid
    t0      = torch.zeros(N_VAL)
    t_dec   = repeat(t_grid, 'k -> b k', b=N_VAL)
    z_tilde = model.dynamic.propagate(t0, model.encoder(x_val[:, 0]), t_dec)  # (b k j l)
    x_tilde = model.decoder(z_tilde)                                          # (b k p)

    # autoencoding path: encode / decode the true state at every time
    z_bar = rearrange(model.encoder(rearrange(x_val, 'b k p -> (b k) p')),
                      '(b k) j l -> b k j l', b=N_VAL)                        # (b k j l)
    x_bar = model.decoder(z_bar)                                              # (b k p)

e_rec, e_prop, e_tot = x_val - x_bar, x_bar - x_tilde, x_val - x_tilde        # (b k p)


One trajectory first. In the latent plane of the top-usage mode, \(\tilde z\) is a logarithmic spiral by construction — the question is whether \(\bar z\) stays on it.

Right: the same trajectory seen in the latent plane of the most used mode — the propagated \(\tilde z\) (crosses) follows an exact logarithmic spiral, the encoded truth \(\bar z\) (dots) should stay on it.





Taking norms in the identity only gives a triangle inequality — the two error vectors can cancel. Squaring restores an exact decomposition:
\[
||x - \tilde x||^2 = ||x - \bar x||^2 + ||\bar x - \tilde x||^2 + 2\,\big\langle x - \bar x,\; \bar x - \tilde x\big\rangle
\]
The cross term measures the cancellation, and is a result in itself:

clearly negative — co-adaptation: the decoder compensates a bias of the dynamic (nothing supervises the blocks separately)
negligible — the single unrolling loss kept the blocks honest

This is the trade-off deep Koopman papers address with separate reconstruction and linearity losses.

title: Koopman Eigenfunctions — An Introduction
text:
Consider a (possibly nonlinear) dynamical system on the state \(\Phi(t)\):
\[
\frac{d\Phi(t)}{dt} = S(\Phi(t))
\]
Integrating from an initial condition \(\Phi_0\) defines the flow \(T\):
\[
T(\Phi_0, t) = \Phi_0 + \int_0^t S(\Phi(t'))\, dt' = \Phi(t)
\]
\(T\) maps an initial condition \(\Phi_0\) and a time \(t\) to the state reached at time \(t\). It is, in general, nonlinear in \(\Phi_0\) — that nonlinearity is exactly the difficulty Koopman theory is built to sidestep.



Koopman eigenfunctions are special observables \(\kPsi_j\) (\(j = 1, 2, 3, \dots\)) with \(\kPsi_j : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) that respect the following relationship :
\[
\kPsi_j(T(\Phi_0, t)) = e^{\klam_j t} \kPsi_j(\Phi_0) \Leftrightarrow \frac{d \kPsi_j(\Phi(t))}{dt} = \klam_j \kPsi_j(\Phi(t))
\]
There could be an infinity of observables for a given dynamic, in practice we will restrict to \(J\).



If our set of eigenfunctions form a basis, every observable \(\kg : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) can be written as a (generally infinite) linear combination of the \(\kPsi_j\):
\[
\kg(\Phi_0) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \kv_j \kPsi_j(\Phi_0)
\]
Once \(\kg\) is expressed in the eigenbasis we can use the eigenfunction property to propagate it forward in time as easily as multiplying each coefficient with an exponential factor :
\[
\kg(T(\Phi_0, t)) = \sum_j \kv_j \kPsi_j(T(\Phi_0, t)) = \sum_j \kv_j e^{\klam_j t} \kPsi_j(\Phi_0)
\]
Although in practice, finding a set of \(\kPsi_j\) that respect the linearity constraint while allowing for a good reconstruction of any observable is not easy, that’s what we are going to see in the next section !






This decomposition induces a new form for the observed dynamic :
\[
\frac{d \kg(\Phi(t))}{dt} = \nabla \kg(\Phi(t)) \cdot S(\Phi(t)) = \sum_j \kv_j \frac{d \kPsi_j(\Phi(t))}{dt} =  \sum_j \kv_j \klam_j \kPsi_j(\Phi(t))
\]






Take the simplest possible case:
\[
\frac{d\Phi(t)}{dt} = \klam \Phi(t)
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
T(\Phi_0, t) = e^{\klam t} \Phi_0
\]
We then introduce a non linear observer \(g : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) and try to express it’s evolution as a sum a weighted koopman eigenfunctions.
Let’s first run it to get a ground-truth trajectory :


Show imports
import torch
from torchdiffeq import odeint
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt




Code
lam = -0.7
phi0 = torch.tensor(1.3)
t_span = (0.0, 10.0)
t_eval = torch.linspace(t_span[0], t_span[1], 100)

f = lambda t, phi: lam * phi

phit = odeint(f, phi0, t_eval)  # true trajectory




Step 1 : From the simulated trajectory we find a set of functions that respect the linearity constraint






\[
\{\kpsi_j\}_{j=1}^{J} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \kpsi_j\big(T(\phi_0, t)\big) = e^{\klam_j t}\, \kpsi_j(\phi_0)
\]



Step 2 : We express our observable function \(\kg\) in this basis \(\kPsi\) :






\[
\kv^\star = \arg\min_{\kv} \int_\phi \Big(\sum_{j=1}^{J} \kv_j\, \kpsi_j(\phi) - \kg(\phi)\Big)^2 d\phi
\]



Step 3 : from the initial observation \(\kg(\phi_0)\) we can forecast :






\[
\kg(\phi_t) \approx \sum_{j=1}^{J} \kv_j\, e^{\klam_j t}\, \kpsi_j(\phi_0)
\]






Try a few candidate observables \(\kg\) and check whether \(\kg(T(\Phi_0,t))\) matches a pure exponential \(e^{\klam_j t} \kg(\Phi_0)\):








Candidate
Test
Eigenfunction?




\(\kg_1(\Phi) = \Phi\)
\(\kg_1(T(\Phi_0,t)) = \kg_1\big(e^{\klam t}\Phi_0\big) = e^{\klam t} \kg_1(\Phi_0)\)
✓


\(\kg_2(\Phi) = \Phi^2\)
\(\kg_2(T(\Phi_0,t)) = \kg_2\big(e^{\klam t}\Phi_0\big) = e^{2\klam t}\Phi_0^2 = e^{2\klam t} \kg_2(\Phi_0)\)
✓


\(\kg_3(\Phi) = \sin(\Phi)\)
\(\kg_3(T(\Phi_0,t)) = \kg_3\big(e^{\klam t}\Phi_0\big) \neq e^{\klam t} \kg_3(\Phi_0)\)
✗



In general, \(\kPsi_k(\Phi) = \Phi^k\) for \(k \in \mathbb{N}\) are Koopman eigenfunctions of this dynamics, with eigenvalue \(k\klam\). Not every observable is an eigenfunction — \(\sin(\Phi)\) is the counter-example.
We can check this numerically: simulate the true trajectory, evaluate a candidate observable along it, and fit an exponential \(\kg(\Phi(t)) = \kg(\Phi_0)\, e^{bt}\). If the candidate is a genuine eigenfunction, the fitted slopes \(b\) at every time point should agree (low variance) and match the predicted eigenvalue.


Code
# model: g(Phi(t)) = g(Phi0) * exp(b*t), with a = g(Phi0) fixed (known), so we only
# fit the slope b of log(g(Phi(t)) / g(Phi0)) = b*t (line through origin). g(Phi(t))
# and g(Phi0) share the same sign here (Phi(t) never crosses zero unless Phi0 = 0).

observables = {
    r"$\Phi(t)^2$": lambda phi: phi ** 2,
    r"$\sin(5\Phi(t))+1$": lambda phi: torch.sin(5 * phi) + 1,
}

obs_fit = {}
for k, g in observables.items():
    gt = g(phit)
    lbds = torch.log(gt[1:] / gt[0]) / t_eval[1:]            # per-timepoint lambda estimate
    fits_each = gt[0] * torch.exp(lbds[:, None] * t_eval)    # (n_lbds, T) - one exp fit per estimate
    fit_t = gt[0] * torch.exp(lbds.mean() * t_eval)          # exp fit using the average lambda
    obs_fit[k] = {"gt": gt, "fit_t": fit_t, "fits_each": fits_each, "lambda": lbds.mean(), "var": lbds.var()}




Show plotting code

Figure 1: Testing candidate observables: \(\Phi(t)^2\) is a true eigenfunction (the faint per-timepoint exp fits collapse onto the average fit), \(\sin(5\Phi(t))+1\) is not (the faint fits fan out).





In this simple case we figure out that \(\kpsi_j(T(t, \phi)) = e^{j\klam t} \kpsi_j(\phi)\ \forall j \in \mathbb{N}\) and thus they are all eigenfunctions with eigenvalues \(j\klam\).


Code
J = 5
Psi = lambda x: torch.stack([x ** k for k in range(0, J)], dim=-1)
lambdas = torch.tensor([k * lam for k in range(J)])





Take \(\kg(\Phi) = \cos(\Phi)\), which is not itself an eigenfunction. The goal is to express it as
\[
\kg(\Phi) = \sum_{j=0}^{J} \kv_j \kpsi_j(\Phi) \qquad \forall\, \Phi \in \mathbb{R}
\]


This amounts to projecting \(\kg\) onto the basis of eigenfunctions, which can be done by least squares:
\[
\kvb = \arg \min_{\kvb} \int_{\phi} \Big(\sum_{j=0}^{J} \kv_j \kpsi_j(\phi) - \kg(\phi)\Big)^2 d\phi
\]
Since the only unknowns are in \(\kvb\), this is a convex problem whenever the \(\kpsi_j\) are linearly independent:
\[
\begin{align}
\kvb &= \arg \min_{\kvb} \int_{\phi} \big(\mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi) \cdot \kv - \kg(\phi)\big)^2 d\phi\\[4pt]
&\int_\phi \mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi)^T\big(\mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi) \cdot \kv^\star - \kg(\phi)\big)\, d\phi \triangleq 0\\[4pt]
\kv^\star &= \Big[\int_\phi \mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi)^T\mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi)\, d\phi\Big]^{-1} \cdot \Big[\int_\phi \mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi)\, \kg(\phi)\, d\phi\Big]
\end{align}
\]
The integrals can be approximated by sample expectations over \(\phi\) :






NoteSpecific projection for this case











NoteReminder: Taylor expansion of a scalar function (centered at a point \(a\))





\[
f(x) = f(a) + (x-a) f'(a) + \frac{(x-a)^2}{2!} f''(a) + \dots
\]



Because \(\kPsi_j(\Phi) = \Phi^j\) is a polynomial basis, we could alternatively use the ordinary Taylor (Maclaurin) series of \(\cos\) centered at \(a=0\):
\[
\cos(\Phi_0) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{\cos^{(j)}(0)}{j!} \Phi_0^j
\qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \kv_j = \frac{\cos^{(j)}(0)}{j!}
\]
This shortcut only works because the eigenbasis happens to coincide with a power series basis; the general least-squares projection above works regardless of the basis.





Code
target_g = lambda phi: torch.cos(phi)

phis = torch.rand(10) * 2.0          # (10,) sample points
psi_phi = Psi(phis)                  # (10, J)
E = psi_phi.T @ psi_phi               # (J, J) Gram matrix
C = psi_phi.T @ target_g(phis)        # (J,)
v_star = torch.linalg.pinv(E) @ C     # least-squares coefficients

pred_g = lambda x: Psi(x) @ v_star

\[
\kg\big(\Phi(t)\big) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \kv_j \kpsi_j\big(\Phi(t)\big) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \kv_j \kpsi_j\big(T(\Phi_0, t)\big) \overset{\text{eig.}}{=} \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \kv_j\, e^{\klam_j t}\, \kpsi_j(\Phi_0)

\[

It seems like a cool way to approximate a physical model — why not apply it to nonlinear, high-dimensional dynamics ?
First, we found the eigenfunctions in an arbitrary way by testing a few candidates; finding meaningful functions that respect linearity in high-dimensional settings is much harder, there might be no closed form for the function and the optimization over functional space is a hard task !
Second, even if we find a set of eigenfunctions, they might not represent the observable of interest well : we need functions that truly capture the target signal.
What’s interesting is the reasoning : eigenfunctions are specific to the dynamical system, but the basis we pick from that infinite family should be tailored to the target observable — a good basis depends on what we’re trying to observe.



Stepping back, the whole procedure above — search for eigenfunctions, then project a target observable onto them — can be seen as a single nested optimization:
\[
\begin{align}
&\{ \kpsi_j \} = \arg \min_{\kpsi_j} \left[ \min_{\kv}\; \int_t \Big(\kg\big(T(t, \phi_0)\big) - \sum_{j=0}^{J} \kv_j\, \kpsi_j\big(T(t, \phi_0)\big)\Big)^2 dt \right] \\
&\text{subject to} \quad \kpsi_j\big(T(t, \phi_0)\big) = e^{\klam_j (t - t_0)}\, \kpsi_j\big(T(t_0, \phi_0)\big)
\end{align}
\]
In a next chapter we will see how this dual optimization procedure relate to koopman based data-driven methods !

title: Koopman Eigenfunctions — An Introduction
text:
Consider a (possibly nonlinear) dynamical system on the state \(\Phi(t)\):
\[
\frac{d\Phi(t)}{dt} = S(\Phi(t))
\]
Integrating from an initial condition \(\Phi_0\) defines the flow \(T\):
\[
T(\Phi_0, t) = \Phi_0 + \int_0^t S(\Phi(t'))\, dt' = \Phi(t)
\]
\(T\) maps an initial condition \(\Phi_0\) and a time \(t\) to the state reached at time \(t\). It is, in general, nonlinear in \(\Phi_0\) — that nonlinearity is exactly the difficulty Koopman theory is built to sidestep.

title: Koopman Eigenfunctions — An Introduction
text:
Koopman eigenfunctions are special observables \(\kPsi_j\) (\(j = 1, 2, 3, \dots\)) with \(\kPsi_j : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) that respect the following relationship :
\[
\kPsi_j(T(\Phi_0, t)) = e^{\klam_j t} \kPsi_j(\Phi_0) \Leftrightarrow \frac{d \kPsi_j(\Phi(t))}{dt} = \klam_j \kPsi_j(\Phi(t))
\]
There could be an infinity of observables for a given dynamic, in practice we will restrict to \(J\).

title: Koopman Eigenfunctions — An Introduction
text:
If our set of eigenfunctions form a basis, every observable \(\kg : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) can be written as a (generally infinite) linear combination of the \(\kPsi_j\):
\[
\kg(\Phi_0) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \kv_j \kPsi_j(\Phi_0)
\]
Once \(\kg\) is expressed in the eigenbasis we can use the eigenfunction property to propagate it forward in time as easily as multiplying each coefficient with an exponential factor :
\[
\kg(T(\Phi_0, t)) = \sum_j \kv_j \kPsi_j(T(\Phi_0, t)) = \sum_j \kv_j e^{\klam_j t} \kPsi_j(\Phi_0)
\]
Although in practice, finding a set of \(\kPsi_j\) that respect the linearity constraint while allowing for a good reconstruction of any observable is not easy, that’s what we are going to see in the next section !






This decomposition induces a new form for the observed dynamic :
\[
\frac{d \kg(\Phi(t))}{dt} = \nabla \kg(\Phi(t)) \cdot S(\Phi(t)) = \sum_j \kv_j \frac{d \kPsi_j(\Phi(t))}{dt} =  \sum_j \kv_j \klam_j \kPsi_j(\Phi(t))
\]

title: Koopman Eigenfunctions — An Introduction
text:
Take the simplest possible case:
\[
\frac{d\Phi(t)}{dt} = \klam \Phi(t)
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
T(\Phi_0, t) = e^{\klam t} \Phi_0
\]
We then introduce a non linear observer \(g : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) and try to express it’s evolution as a sum a weighted koopman eigenfunctions.
Let’s first run it to get a ground-truth trajectory :


Show imports

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt




Code

\]



Step 2 : We express our observable function \(\kg\) in this basis \(\kPsi\) :






\[
\kv^\star = \arg\min_{\kv} \int_\phi \Big(\sum_{j=1}^{J} \kv_j\, \kpsi_j(\phi) - \kg(\phi)\Big)^2 d\phi
\]



Step 3 : from the initial observation \(\kg(\phi_0)\) we can forecast :






\[
\kg(\phi_t) \approx \sum_{j=1}^{J} \kv_j\, e^{\klam_j t}\, \kpsi_j(\phi_0)
\]






Try a few candidate observables \(\kg\) and check whether \(\kg(T(\Phi_0,t))\) matches a pure exponential \(e^{\klam_j t} \kg(\Phi_0)\):








Candidate
Test
Eigenfunction?




\(\kg_1(\Phi) = \Phi\)
\(\kg_1(T(\Phi_0,t)) = \kg_1\big(e^{\klam t}\Phi_0\big) = e^{\klam t} \kg_1(\Phi_0)\)
✓


\(\kg_2(\Phi) = \Phi^2\)
\(\kg_2(T(\Phi_0,t)) = \kg_2\big(e^{\klam t}\Phi_0\big) = e^{2\klam t}\Phi_0^2 = e^{2\klam t} \kg_2(\Phi_0)\)
✓


\(\kg_3(\Phi) = \sin(\Phi)\)
\(\kg_3(T(\Phi_0,t)) = \kg_3\big(e^{\klam t}\Phi_0\big) \neq e^{\klam t} \kg_3(\Phi_0)\)
✗



In general, \(\kPsi_k(\Phi) = \Phi^k\) for \(k \in \mathbb{N}\) are Koopman eigenfunctions of this dynamics, with eigenvalue \(k\klam\). Not every observable is an eigenfunction — \(\sin(\Phi)\) is the counter-example.
We can check this numerically: simulate the true trajectory, evaluate a candidate observable along it, and fit an exponential \(\kg(\Phi(t)) = \kg(\Phi_0)\, e^{bt}\). If the candidate is a genuine eigenfunction, the fitted slopes \(b\) at every time point should agree (low variance) and match the predicted eigenvalue.

Take \(\kg(\Phi) = \cos(\Phi)\), which is not itself an eigenfunction. The goal is to express it as
\[
\kg(\Phi) = \sum_{j=0}^{J} \kv_j \kpsi_j(\Phi) \qquad \forall\, \Phi \in \mathbb{R}
\]


This amounts to projecting \(\kg\) onto the basis of eigenfunctions, which can be done by least squares:
\[
\kvb = \arg \min_{\kvb} \int_{\phi} \Big(\sum_{j=0}^{J} \kv_j \kpsi_j(\phi) - \kg(\phi)\Big)^2 d\phi
\]
Since the only unknowns are in \(\kvb\), this is a convex problem whenever the \(\kpsi_j\) are linearly independent:
\[
\begin{align}
\kvb &= \arg \min_{\kvb} \int_{\phi} \big(\mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi) \cdot \kv - \kg(\phi)\big)^2 d\phi\\[4pt]
&\int_\phi \mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi)^T\big(\mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi) \cdot \kv^\star - \kg(\phi)\big)\, d\phi \triangleq 0\\[4pt]
\kv^\star &= \Big[\int_\phi \mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi)^T\mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi)\, d\phi\Big]^{-1} \cdot \Big[\int_\phi \mathbf{\kPsi}(\phi)\, \kg(\phi)\, d\phi\Big]
\end{align}
\]
The integrals can be approximated by sample expectations over \(\phi\) :






NoteSpecific projection for this case











NoteReminder: Taylor expansion of a scalar function (centered at a point \(a\))





\[
f(x) = f(a) + (x-a) f'(a) + \frac{(x-a)^2}{2!} f''(a) + \dots
\]



Because \(\kPsi_j(\Phi) = \Phi^j\) is a polynomial basis, we could alternatively use the ordinary Taylor (Maclaurin) series of \(\cos\) centered at \(a=0\):
\[
\cos(\Phi_0) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{\cos^{(j)}(0)}{j!} \Phi_0^j
\qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \kv_j = \frac{\cos^{(j)}(0)}{j!}
\]
This shortcut only works because the eigenbasis happens to coincide with a power series basis; the general least-squares projection above works regardless of the basis.

Can Koopman eigenfunctions be complex? — a follow-up on why \(\kpsi_j\), \(\kv_j\), \(\klam_j\) are generally complex-valued even when the observable \(\kg\) is real.

title: Koopman with complex eigenfunctions
text:
In many systems koopman models are going to live in complex space, even if the physical variable is in real space. This impact the way we do our temporal integration and our reconstruction.
@dataclass
class ComplexPoint:
    a: float
    b: float
    c : float
    w : float
    

    def f(self, t, x):
        """x (..., 2) -> dx/dt (..., 2)"""
        x1, x2 = x[..., 0], x[..., 1]
        xp1 = self.a * x1 - self.w * x2 + self.w * self.c * x1**2

        xp2 = (
            self.w * x1
            + self.a * x2
            + self.a * self.c * x1**2
            - 2 * self.c * self.w * x1 * x2
            + 2 * self.c**2 * self.w * x1**3
        )

        return torch.stack([xp1, xp2], dim=-1)

fp = ComplexPoint(1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0)

x0 = torch.tensor([1., 2.])
t_int = torch.linspace(0, 2, 100)
x_gt = odeint(fp.f, x0, t_int)
-> Here we show trajectory of x_gt


\[
\psi_j(x_t) = e^{\lambda_j t}\,\psi_j(x_0) = e^{(\gamma+\omega i)t}\, r_j(x_0)\, e^{i\varphi_j(x_0)} =  r_j(x_0)\,e^{\gamma t }\, e^{i(\varphi_j(x_0) +\omega t)}
\]
Thus we just have a scaling in magnitude and a shift in phase. Those two isolated contribution of the dynamic makes them easier to apply in polar representation than in coordinates one.
In order to check if observed values are following a linear relationship we can :

Check if their magnitude have an exponential relationship \(\log(\frac{r(t)}{r(0)}) = \gamma t\)
Check if their angle have a common shift : \(\phi (t) - \phi(0) = \operatorname{mod}_{2\pi}(\omega t)\)

# True eigenfunction
def psi(x):
    x1, x2 = x[...,0], x[...,1]
    return torch.complex(x1, x2 - fp.c*x1**2)



# Test one (not an eigenfunction)
def f(x):
    x1, x2 = x[...,0], x[...,1]
    return torch.complex(x1 + x2, x1- x2)

Once we have the eigenfunctions and values we can use them to project in future timestep :

title: Matrix Exponential vs Numerical Integration
text:
In this tutorial we study the linear ODE
\[\frac{dz}{dt} = Az, \quad z(0) = z_0\]
where \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}\). The behavior of trajectories is entirely governed by the eigenvalues of \(A\). We illustrate with three canonical cases:









Case
Matrix
Eigenvalues
Behavior




Stable node
\(A_1 = \begin{pmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -0.5\end{pmatrix}\)
\(-2,\ -0.5\)
Trajectories collapse to the origin along eigenvector directions


Center
\(A_2 = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{pmatrix}\)
\(\pm 2i\)
Closed orbits, energy is conserved


Stable degenerate node
\(A_3 = \begin{pmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}\)
\(-1\) (double)
Converges to origin with a \(t e^{-t}\) transient; non-diagonalizable





imports
import numpy as np
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from torchdiffeq import odeint



A1 = torch.tensor([[-2.0, 0.0],
                   [ 0.0,-0.5]], dtype=torch.float64)   # stable node

A2 = torch.tensor([[ 0.0,-2.0],
                   [ 2.0, 0.0]], dtype=torch.float64)   # center

A3 = torch.tensor([[-1.0, 1.0],
                   [ 0.0,-1.0]], dtype=torch.float64)   # stable degenerate node (Jordan block)

cases = [("Stable node",            A1),
         ("Center",                 A2),
         ("Stable degenerate node", A3)]
















NoteWhy can’t we have one real and one imaginary eigenvalue?





For a real \(2 \times 2\) matrix, the characteristic polynomial is
\[\det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - \operatorname{tr}(A)\,\lambda + \det(A) = 0\]
with discriminant \(\delta = \operatorname{tr}(A)^2 - 4\det(A)\). The three cases are:
\[\lambda = \frac{\operatorname{tr}(A)}{2} \pm \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\delta} & \delta > 0 \quad \text{(two real eigenvalues)} \\ \frac{i}{2}\sqrt{-\delta} & \delta < 0 \quad \text{(complex conjugate pair)} \\ 0 & \delta = 0 \quad \text{(one repeated real eigenvalue)} \end{cases}\]
Complex eigenvalues always come as conjugate pairs \(a \pm bi\), so it is impossible to have one purely real and one purely imaginary eigenvalue for a real matrix.






We have two ways to propagate a state from \(z_0\) to time \(t\):
\[z(t) = \underbrace{\texttt{odeint}(A,\, z_0,\, t)}_{\text{numerical integration}} \qquad \longleftrightarrow \qquad z(t) = \underbrace{e^{At}\,z_0}_{\text{matrix exponential}}\]
What is the connection between the two? We denote by \(z_e\) the state obtained by the Euler scheme with step size \(\delta_t\):
\[z_e(\delta_t) = z_0 + \delta_t A z_0 = (I + \delta_t A)\,z_0\]
Applying the same step again from \(z_e(\delta_t)\):
\[z_e(2\delta_t) = (I + \delta_t A)\,z_e(\delta_t) = (I + \delta_t A)^2\,z_0 = z_0 + 2\delta_t A z_0 + \delta_t^2 A^2 z_0\]
By induction over \(K\) steps:
\[z_e(K\delta_t) = (I + \delta_t A)^K\,z_0\]
Setting \(t = K\delta_t\) (i.e. \(K = t/\delta_t\)) and taking \(\delta_t \to 0\):
\[z_e(t) = \left(I + \frac{t}{K} A\right)^K z_0 \xrightarrow[K \to \infty]{} e^{At}\,z_0\]
This is exactly the standard limit definition of the matrix exponential. The matrix exponential is the continuous limit of the Euler scheme — accuracy degrades as \(\delta_t\) grows.


Euler vs exact — plot

T     = 4.0
t_ref = torch.linspace(0, T, 500, dtype=torch.float64)

# exact solution via matrix exponential for each t
def exact(A, t, z0):
    return (torch.linalg.matrix_exp(A[None] * t[:, None, None]) @ z0).numpy()

# euler with K steps
def euler(A, t_grid, z0):
    return odeint(lambda t, z: A @ z, z0, t_grid, method='euler').numpy()

step_sizes = {f"$\\delta_t={T/10:.2f}$":  torch.linspace(0, T, 10,  dtype=torch.float64),
              f"$\\delta_t={T/50:.2f}$":  torch.linspace(0, T, 50,  dtype=torch.float64),
              f"$\\delta_t={T/500:.3f}$": torch.linspace(0, T, 500, dtype=torch.float64)}
colors_euler = ["#e74c3c", "#e67e22", "#2ecc71"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.5))
for ax, (title, A) in zip(axes, cases):
    z_ex = exact(A, t_ref, z0)
    ax.plot(z_ex[:,0], z_ex[:,1], 'k-', lw=2, label='exact $e^{At}z_0$')
    for (label, t_grid), color in zip(step_sizes.items(), colors_euler):

        ax.plot(z_eu[:,0], z_eu[:,1], '--', color=color, lw=1.2, label=f'Euler {label}')
    ax.plot(*z0.numpy(), 'ko', markersize=5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel('$z_1$'); ax.set_ylabel('$z_2$')
    ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

axes[0].legend(fontsize=7, loc='best')
fig.suptitle('Euler vs exact $e^{At}z_0$ — three step sizes', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')

title: Matrix Exponential vs Numerical Integration
text:
Diagonalization
If \(A = VDV^{-1}\), then \(e^{At} = V e^{Dt} V^{-1}\), where \(e^{Dt}\) is cheap to compute (diagonal).
For non-diagonalizable \(A\) this fails; Schur decomposition is the fallback.

L, V = torch.linalg.eig(A_ex)
assert torch.linalg.cond(V) < 1e10, 'Matrix A is not diagonalizable'

# Note that V and L entries are potentially complex, although z_t are real in any way as A is real entry
# Thus to allow computation you need to convert the initial condition to complex and then you can safely convert back to real

z_t  = (V @ torch.diag(torch.exp(L * t_ex)) @ torch.linalg.inv(V) @ z0_ex.cdouble()).real

✓ once you have computed the diagonal form you can evaluate the exponential for free for any \(z_0\) and \(t\)
✗ \(A\) needs to be diagonalizable

title: Matrix Exponential vs Numerical Integration
text:
Approximate \(e^{At}\)
Approximates \(e^{At}\) as a ratio of matrix polynomials with a scaling-and-squaring step for large \(\|At\|\).

expAt = torch.linalg.matrix_exp(A_ex * t_ex)   # (Apparently what is done in pytorch is similar to Padé)
z_t   = expAt @ z0_ex                            # reuse for any z0

✓ works for any matrix (even non-diagonalizable)
✓ once you have computed \(e^{At}\) you can evaluate \(e^{At}z_0\) for free for any \(z_0\)
✗ need to restart the approximation for every new \(t\)

title: Matrix Exponential vs Numerical Integration
text:
Approximate \(e^{At}z_0\)
We remember that :
\[
\exp(At)z_0 = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k!} A^k t^k z_0
\]
And that the terms of the sum eventually decay (as \(k\) increases the \(k!\) term dominates \(\|A^k z_0\|_2 \leq \sigma_{\max}^k \|z_0\|_2\))
Thus, rather than forming the full \(n \times n\) matrix \(e^{At}\), we could build a basis as \(\mathcal{K}_m = \text{span}\{z_0,\, Az_0,\, A^2z_0,\,\ldots\}\) of dimension \(m \ll n\) and compute :
\[e^{At}z_0 \approx \sum_{j=0}^{M} \frac{1}{j!} K_j t^j\]
This is the general idea, in practice, the Krylov method builds an orthonormal basis of \(\mathcal{K}_m\) to avoid the numerical instability of summing the raw \(A^j z_0\) terms directly.
PyTorch currently has no built-in function for this, but we can use the one from scipy:

from scipy.sparse.linalg import expm_multiply
z_t = expm_multiply(A_ex.numpy() * t_ex.item(), z0_ex.numpy())

✓ works for any matrix (even non-diagonalizable)
✓ once you have computed the basis you can evaluate \(e^{At}z_0\) for free for any \(t\)
✗ need to rebuild the basis for every new \(z_0\)

title: Matrix Exponential vs Numerical Integration
text:
Numerical integration (odeint)
Solves \(\dot{z} = Az\) by stepping through intermediate times from \(z_0\) to \(t\). Step size is constrained by the stiffness of \(A\) (ratio of largest to smallest \(|\lambda|\)). Naturally efficient for successive \(t\) values on the same trajectory since all intermediate states are already computed.

z_t    = odeint(lambda t, z: A_ex @ z, z0_ex, torch.tensor([0.0, t_ex]))[-1]

✓ works with \(\dot{z}(t) = A(t) z(t)\) (time-varying linear dynamics)
✓ works for any matrix (even non-diagonalizable), although slow if \(\kappa(A)\) is large
✗ need to restart for every new \(t\) and \(z_0\)

title: Koopman with complex eigenfunctions
text:
In many systems Koopman models live in complex space, even when the physical variables are real. This impacts the way we do our temporal integration and our reconstruction.
We illustrate this on the nonlinear system
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot{x}_1 &= a\,x_1 - \omega\,x_2 + \omega c\,x_1^2 \\
\dot{x}_2 &= \omega\,x_1 + a\,x_2 + a c\,x_1^2 - 2 c \omega\,x_1 x_2 + 2 c^2 \omega\,x_1^3
\end{aligned}
\]
whose flow we integrate below with parameters \((a, \omega, c) = (1, 4, 3)\).


Show imports
import torch
from torchdiffeq import odeint
from dataclasses import dataclass
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from einops import rearrange




Code
@dataclass
class ComplexPoint:
    a: float
    c: float
    w: float

    def f(self, t, x):
        """x (..., 2) -> dx/dt (..., 2)"""
        x1, x2 = x[..., 0], x[..., 1]
        xp1 = self.a * x1 - self.w * x2 + self.w * self.c * x1**2

        xp2 = (
            self.w * x1
            + self.a * x2
            + self.a * self.c * x1**2
            - 2 * self.c * self.w * x1 * x2
            + 2 * self.c**2 * self.w * x1**3
        )

        return torch.stack([xp1, xp2], dim=-1)

fp = ComplexPoint(1.0, 3.0, 4.0)

x0 = torch.tensor([1., 2.])
t_int = torch.linspace(0, 2, 100)
x_gt = odeint(fp.f, x0, t_int)

1 Temporal evolution
\[
\kpsi_j(x_t) = e^{\klam_j t}\,\kpsi_j(x_0) = e^{(\gamma+\omega i)t}\, r_j(x_0)\, e^{i\varphi_j(x_0)} =  r_j(x_0)\,e^{\gamma t }\, e^{i(\varphi_j(x_0) +\omega t)}
\]
Thus we just have a scaling in magnitude and a shift in phase. These two contributions decouple, which makes the dynamics easier to apply in a polar representation than in Cartesian coordinates.
In order to check if observed values follow a linear relationship we can:

Check if their magnitude has an exponential relationship \(\log(\frac{r(t)}{r(0)}) = \gamma t\)
Check if their angle has a common shift: \(\varphi(t) - \varphi(0) = \operatorname{mod}_{2\pi}(\omega t)\)

As in the nonlinear example we test two candidates: the true eigenfunction \(\kpsi\) and a guess \(f\) which is not one.


Code
# True eigenfunction
def psi(x):
    x1, x2 = x[..., 0], x[..., 1]
    return torch.complex(x1, x2 - fp.c * x1**2)

# Test one (not an eigenfunction)
def f(x):
    x1, x2 = x[..., 0], x[..., 1]
    return torch.complex(x1 + x2, x1 - x2)

Here we need to adapt our technique to test if the projected trajectory follows a linear dynamic in complex space:


Code
def polar_rates(px):
    """Per-timepoint estimates of (gamma, omega) from a complex sequence px (T,)"""
    gammas = torch.log(px[1:].abs() / px[0].abs()) / t_int[1:]
    angles = torch.from_numpy(np.unwrap(px.angle().numpy())).float()
    omegas = (angles[1:] - angles[0]) / t_int[1:]
    return gammas, omegas

gammas, omegas = polar_rates(psi(x_gt))
gamma, omega = gammas.mean(), omegas.mean()

psi_0 = psi(x_gt[0])

2 Reconstruction
As we showed in the complex notebook, Koopman eigenfunctions always come with their conjugate, which lets us retrieve the real state at reconstruction time. As we want to learn \(\kv_j = \alpha_j + \beta_j i\) which is the weight given to an eigenfunction in the reconstruction we can show:
\[
\begin{align}
\min_{\kvb \in \mathbb C^{J}} ||\kg(x) - \sum_j^J \kv_j \kpsi_j(x)|| &= ||\kg(x) - \sum_j^{J/2} \big(\kv_j \kpsi_j(x) + \bar{\kv}_j \bar{\kpsi}_j(x)\big)||\\
&= ||\kg(x) - \sum_j^{J/2} \big((\alpha_j + \beta_j i)(a_j(x) + b_j(x)i) +  (\alpha_j - \beta_j i)(a_j(x) - b_j(x)i)\big)||\\
&= ||\kg(x) - 2\sum_j^{J/2} \big(\alpha_j a_j(x) - \beta_j b_j(x)\big)||\\
\end{align}
\]
So we end up doing a linear regression with the real and imaginary parts of the eigenfunction. The good news is that if we didn’t include the conjugate of \(\kpsi_j\) in our chosen eigenbasis, this method doesn’t need it: it leads to the same reconstruction as if we had. And if the conjugate is present, the weights simply adapt.






NoteNote on the eigenlattice





We can use the eigenlattice property to improve the representation of \(\kg(x)\). In the previous section we stated that each eigenfunction has its conjugate and that we didn’t need to include it given the way we do reconstruction. Although something interesting is that they can take part in the eigenlattice and that \(\kpsi_j \bar{\kpsi}_j\) is an eigenfunction too! Which increases the expressivity of the eigenspace.





Code
xs = torch.randn(10, 2)
Psi = lambda x: torch.stack([psi(x), psi(x)**2, psi(x) * psi(x).conj()], dim=-1)  # (n, J)

def complex_to_component(z):
    """
        z (n, J) complex -> (n, 2J) real

    Take a complex tensor and return a real tensor with the two components stacked
    """
    r = torch.view_as_real(z)
    r_flat = rearrange(r, 'n J c -> n (J c)')
    return r_flat

V = torch.linalg.lstsq(complex_to_component(Psi(xs)), xs).solution.T

tilde_x_gt = complex_to_component(Psi(x_gt)) @ V.T




Show plotting code

axs[0].set_title("True")
axs[1].set_title("Reconstruction")
axs[0].scatter(*x_gt.T)
axs[1].scatter(*tilde_x_gt.T)
for ax in axs:
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$x_1$")
axs[0].set_ylabel(r"$x_2$")
fig.tight_layout()

3 Forecasting summary
So we can summarise the forecast with the following figure: compute the eigenfunctions, project them forward with the polar form and recompose linearly to form the physical state:







Code
Gammas = torch.tensor([gamma, 2 * gamma, 2 * gamma])  # (J)
Omegas = torch.tensor([omega, 2 * omega, 0])  # (J)


def forecast_from(x0):
    """Koopman forecast of the whole trajectory from an initial state x0."""
    psi_0 = Psi(x0)
    psi_0_r, psi_0_w = psi_0.abs(), psi_0.angle()  # (J), (J)

    psi_r = torch.exp(Gammas[None] * t_int[:, None]) * psi_0_r[None]  # (T, J)
    psi_w = psi_0_w[None] + Omegas * t_int[:, None]  # (T, J)

    psi_t = complex_to_component(torch.polar(psi_r, psi_w))  # (T, (2*J))
    return psi_t @ V.T


# several initial states, each giving its own trajectory
x0s = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [-1.0, 1.0], [0.5, -0.5], [-0.5, -1.5]])
t_int = torch.linspace(0, 0.2, 100)

gts = [odeint(fp.f, x0, t_int) for x0 in x0s]      # ground-truth integration
forecasts = [forecast_from(x0) for x0 in x0s]      # Koopman forecast from x0

axs[0].set_title("Ground truth")
axs[1].set_title("Koopman forecasts")

for k, (x_true, x_fore) in enumerate(zip(gts, forecasts)):
    color = f"C{k}"
    axs[0].scatter(*x_true.T, s=10, color=color, label=f"traj {k}")
    axs[1].scatter(*x_fore.T, s=10, color=color)
    for ax in axs:
        ax.scatter(*x0s[k], color=color, edgecolors="k", s=60, zorder=3)

axs[0].legend()
for ax in axs:
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$x_1$")
axs[0].set_ylabel(r"$x_2$")

plt.show()

title: Koopman Eigenfunctions — A Nonlinear Example
text:
In the introduction we applied the Koopman decomposition to a scalar linear ODE. Here we do the full loop — test eigenfunctions, decompose an observable, forecast — on a genuinely nonlinear system, chosen because its eigenfunctions have a closed form:
\[
\frac{d\Phi(t)}{dt} = S(\Phi(t)), \qquad
S(x_1, x_2) =
\begin{pmatrix}
\mu\, x_1 \\
\klam\, (x_2 - x_1^2)
\end{pmatrix}
\]
The \(x_1^2\) term makes the flow nonlinear. Let’s simulate a ground-truth trajectory:


Show imports
import torch
from torchdiffeq import odeint
from dataclasses import dataclass
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt




Code
@dataclass
class FixedPoint:
    mu: float
    lbd: float

    def f(self, t, x):
        """x (..., 2) -> dx/dt (..., 2)"""
        x1, x2 = x[..., 0], x[..., 1]
        xp1 = self.mu * x1
        xp2 = self.lbd * (x2 - x1**2)
        return torch.stack([xp1, xp2], dim=-1)

fp = FixedPoint(mu=1.0, lbd=3.0)

x0 = torch.tensor([1., 2.])
t_int = torch.linspace(0, 1, 10)
x_gt = odeint(fp.f, x0, t_int)




Show plotting code
plt.figure(figsize=(5, 4))
plt.scatter(*x_gt.T, c=t_int)
plt.xlabel(r"$x_1$")
plt.ylabel(r"$x_2$")
plt.colorbar(label="t")
plt.show()

title: Learning Linear Dynamics
text:
In the previous post we studied how to evaluate \(e^{At}z_0\) efficiently. Here we flip the question:

Given observations \(z(t_1), \ldots, z(t_n)\) of a trajectory driven by \(\dot{z} = Az\), recover the matrix \(A\).

This is the core sub-problem in system identification, Koopman operator learning, and physics-informed machine learning. We compare four approaches that differ in their data requirements, computational cost, and sensitivity to noise.


We use a stable node with off-diagonal coupling as the true system and observe the trajectory at \(n = 4\) uniformly-spaced time points. The eigenvalues are \(-0.1\) and \(-1\) — real, stable, with well-separated time scales.
\[A = \begin{pmatrix}-0.4 & 0.6 \\ 0.3 & -0.7\end{pmatrix}, \quad z_0 = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1.5\end{pmatrix}\]

import torch
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from torchdiffeq import odeint
from tqdm import tqdm
from scipy.interpolate import CubicSpline
from scipy.linalg import logm

plt.rcParams.update({
    'figure.dpi': 110,
    'axes.grid': True,
    'grid.alpha': 0.25,
    'axes.spines.top': False,
    'axes.spines.right': False,
    'font.size': 10,
})



A = torch.tensor([[-0.4,  0.6],
                   [ 0.3, -0.7]], dtype=torch.float64)   # stable node, eigs = -0.1, -1.0

# Generate true points
T_gt, dt_gt = 2.0, 0.5
z0 = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.5], dtype=torch.float64)
t_gt = torch.linspace(0, T_gt, int(T_gt//dt_gt))

z_gt = torch.matrix_exp(A[None]*t_gt[:, None, None])@z0



plotting helpers
def _streamplot(ax, M, color, alpha=0.45, density=0.9,
                xlim=(-0.2, 1.7), ylim=(-0.2, 1.9), n_grid=20):
    M_np = M.real.detach().numpy() if torch.is_complex(M) else M.detach().numpy()
    xs = np.linspace(*xlim, n_grid)
    ys = np.linspace(*ylim, n_grid)
    X, Y = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)
    pts = np.stack([X.ravel(), Y.ravel()], axis=1)
    UV = pts @ M_np.T
    sp = ax.streamplot(xs, ys,
                       UV[:, 0].reshape(n_grid, n_grid),
                       UV[:, 1].reshape(n_grid, n_grid),
                       density=density, color=color,
                       linewidth=0.7, arrowsize=0.6)
    sp.lines.set_alpha(alpha)
    sp.arrows.set_alpha(alpha)
    ax.set_xlim(xlim); ax.set_ylim(ylim)
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
    ax.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.3)
    ax.axvline(0, color='k', lw=0.3)


def plot_results(metrics, B, z_pred, z_gt, t_gt, title=None):
    has_metrics = isinstance(metrics, list) and len(metrics) > 0
    ncols = 3 if has_metrics else 2
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, ncols, figsize=(3 * ncols, 3.5))
    if title:
        fig.suptitle(title, fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')

    col = 0

    # training metrics (gradient-based approaches only)
    if has_metrics:
        ax = axes[col]; col += 1
        c1, c2 = 'tab:green', 'tab:purple'
        ax.plot([l['loss'] for l in metrics], color=c1)
        ax.set_xlabel('Epoch'); ax.set_ylabel('Loss', color=c1)
        ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor=c1)
        ax2 = ax.twinx()
        ax2.plot([l['forb'] for l in metrics], color=c2)
        ax2.set_ylabel(r'$\|A - B\|_F^2$', color=c2)
        ax2.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor=c2)
        ax.set_title('Training metrics')

    # trajectory comparison
    ax = axes[col]; col += 1
    t_np = t_gt.numpy()
    ax.scatter(t_np, z_gt[:, 0].detach(), color='tab:blue',   s=55, zorder=3, label='$z_1$ gt')
    ax.scatter(t_np, z_gt[:, 1].detach(), color='tab:orange', s=55, zorder=3, label='$z_2$ gt')
    ax.plot(t_np, z_pred[:, 0].detach(), color='tab:blue',   ls='--', lw=1.8, label='$z_1$ pred')
    ax.plot(t_np, z_pred[:, 1].detach(), color='tab:orange', ls='--', lw=1.8, label='$z_2$ pred')
    ax.set_xlabel('$t$'); ax.set_title('Trajectory')
    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc='best')

    # phase portrait: true A (grey) vs fitted B (red)
    ax = axes[col]
    _streamplot(ax, A, color='#aaaaaa', alpha=0.4)
    _streamplot(ax, B, color='tab:red',  alpha=0.6)
    t_fine = torch.linspace(0, T_gt, 300, dtype=torch.float64)
    B_safe = B.real if torch.is_complex(B) else B
    with torch.no_grad():
        z_true_fine = odeint(lambda t, x: A       @ x, z0, t_fine).numpy()
        z_pred_fine = odeint(lambda t, x: B_safe  @ x, z0, t_fine).numpy()
    ax.plot(z_true_fine[:, 0], z_true_fine[:, 1], color='#444444', lw=1.8, label='true $A$')
    ax.plot(z_pred_fine[:, 0], z_pred_fine[:, 1], color='royalblue', ls='--', lw=1.8, label='fitted $B$')
    ax.scatter(*z0.numpy(), color='k', s=60, zorder=5)
    ax.set_title('Phase portrait'); ax.legend(fontsize=8)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def _streamplot(ax, M, color, alpha=0.45, density=0.9,
                xlim=(-0.2, 1.7), ylim=(-0.2, 1.9), n_grid=20):
    M_np = M.real.detach().numpy() if torch.is_complex(M) else M.detach().numpy()
    xs = np.linspace(*xlim, n_grid)
    ys = np.linspace(*ylim, n_grid)
    X, Y = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)
    pts = np.stack([X.ravel(), Y.ravel()], axis=1)
    UV = pts @ M_np.T
    sp = ax.streamplot(xs, ys,
                       UV[:, 0].reshape(n_grid, n_grid),
                       UV[:, 1].reshape(n_grid, n_grid),
                       density=density, color=color,
                       linewidth=0.7, arrowsize=0.6)
    sp.lines.set_alpha(alpha)
    sp.arrows.set_alpha(alpha)
    ax.set_xlim(xlim); ax.set_ylim(ylim)
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
    ax.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.3)
    ax.axvline(0, color='k', lw=0.3)


def plot_results(metrics, B, z_pred, z_gt, t_gt, title=None):
    has_metrics = isinstance(metrics, list) and len(metrics) > 0
    ncols = 3 if has_metrics else 2
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, ncols, figsize=(3 * ncols, 3.5))
    if title:

        ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor=c1)
        ax2 = ax.twinx()
        ax2.plot([l['forb'] for l in metrics], color=c2)
        ax2.set_ylabel(r'$\|A - B\|_F^2$', color=c2)
        ax2.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor=c2)
        ax.set_title('Training metrics')

    # trajectory comparison
    ax = axes[col]; col += 1
    t_np = t_gt.numpy()

    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc='best')

    ax = axes[col]
    _streamplot(ax, A, color='#aaaaaa', alpha=0.4)
    _streamplot(ax, B, color='tab:red',  alpha=0.6)
    t_fine = torch.linspace(0, T_gt, 300, dtype=torch.float64)

title: Learning Linear Dynamics
text:
Idea
Directly optimise \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}\) to minimise the squared error at every observed time:
\[\mathcal{L}(B) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left\| e^{B t_i} z_0 - z(t_i) \right\|^2\]
Gradients flow through torch.matrix_exp (which uses a Padé approximation internally). No structure is imposed on \(B\) — stability, symmetry, sparsity are unconstrained.
Data requirement: a single trajectory.

title: Learning Linear Dynamics
text:
Code

B = torch.randn((2,2), dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
opt = torch.optim.SGD([B], lr=0.005)

def step() :
    opt.zero_grad()
    z_pred = torch.matrix_exp(B[None]*t_gt[:, None, None])@z0
    L = (z_pred - z_gt).pow(2).sum()
    L.backward()
    opt.step()
    return {'loss' : L.item(), 'forb' : (A - B).pow(2).sum()}

metrics = [step() for i in tqdm(range(1000))]



plot
with torch.no_grad() :
    z_pred = torch.matrix_exp(B[None]*t_gt[:, None, None])@z0
    plot_results(metrics, B, z_pred, z_gt, t_gt, title='Approach 1 — Gradient descent on expm')

title: Learning Linear Dynamics
text:
Idea
Same loss as Approach 1, but the forward pass uses a numerical ODE solver instead of the closed-form matrix exponential:
\[\mathcal{L}(B) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left\| \texttt{odeint}(B,\, z_0,\, t_i) - z(t_i) \right\|^2\]
Gradients propagate through the integrator via the adjoint method. The two approaches are equivalent in theory but differ numerically: odeint introduces discretisation error that can smooth the loss landscape.
Data requirement: a single trajectory.

title: Learning Linear Dynamics
text:
Idea
Since \(\dot{z}(t) = Az(t)\) holds pointwise, stacking observations column-wise gives a linear equation in \(A\):
\[\dot{Z} = A Z, \qquad Z = \bigl[z(t_1) \;\cdots\; z(t_n)\bigr] \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times n}\]
The least-squares solution is:
\[B = \dot{\hat{Z}}\, Z^{\dagger}\]
where \(Z^{\dagger} = Z^\top(ZZ^\top)^{-1}\) and \(\dot{\hat{Z}}\) is estimated by differentiating a cubic spline fitted to the observations. No gradient descent is required — this is a single linear solve.
The quality of the estimate depends on how faithfully the spline captures \(\dot{z}\), which degrades as observations become sparser.
Data requirement: a single trajectory.

title: Learning Linear Dynamics
text:
Idea
With \(K\) trajectories from different initial conditions, all observed at the same time \(t\), stack them column-wise:
\[Z(t) = e^{At} Z_0, \qquad Z_0 = \bigl[z_0^{(1)} \;\cdots\; z_0^{(K)}\bigr] \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times K}\]
For \(K \geq p\) with \(Z_0\) full row rank, the transition matrix \(e^{At}\) is identified by least squares, and \(A\) is recovered via the matrix logarithm:
\[e^{At} = Z(t)\, Z_0^{\dagger} \implies A = \frac{1}{t}\,\operatorname{logm}\!\bigl(Z(t)\, Z_0^{\dagger}\bigr)\]
This is a closed-form, one-shot estimate — no gradient descent, no derivative estimation.






WarningBranch cut



logm applies the principal matrix logarithm, which recovers \(\lambda_k t\) from \(e^{\lambda_k t}\) only when \(|\operatorname{Im}(\lambda_k t)| < \pi\). For oscillatory modes with frequency \(\omega\) this requires \(\omega t < \pi\). Use a small observation time \(t\) to stay on the correct branch.


Data requirement: \(K \geq p\) trajectories from linearly independent initial conditions.

title: Learning Linear Dynamics
section: Approach 5 : find the closest diagonal dynamic
text:
Approach 5 : find the closest diagonal dynamic
One can assume that the dynamic is diagonal (each component is independent).
In this case:
\[
z_{k,p}(t) = e^{\lambda_p t}\, z_{k,p}(0) \qquad \forall\, t,\, k
\]
Thus this amounts to solving:
\[
\lambda_p = \underset{\lambda_p}{\operatorname{argmin}} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{S}} \sum_{i} \bigl(z_{k,p}(t_i) - e^{\lambda_p t_i} z_{k,p}(0)\bigr)^2
\]
Taking the log of the model linearises the problem in \(\lambda_p\):
\[
\lambda_p = \underset{\lambda_p}{\operatorname{argmin}} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{S}} \sum_{i} \bigl(\log z_{k,p}(t_i) - \lambda_p\, t_i - \log z_{k,p}(0)\bigr)^2
\]
We can solve this in matrix form. Stacking all time points into \(\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}\) and defining \(L_{i,p} = \log z_p(t_i) - \log z_p(0)\):
\[
\mathbf{t}\,[\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p] = L \implies \Lambda = \mathbf{t}^{\dagger}\, L
\]

if (z_gt > 0).all() and (z0 > 0).all():
    l_gt = torch.log(z_gt)
    l_0  = torch.log(z0)
    lbd  = (torch.linalg.pinv(t_gt[:, None].to(torch.float64)) @ (l_gt - l_0)).squeeze()
    B    = torch.diag(lbd)
else:
    print("Approach 5 not applicable: spiral trajectory goes negative — log undefined.")
    B = torch.full((2, 2), float('nan'), dtype=torch.float64)

metrics = {}



plot
with torch.no_grad() :
    z_pred = odeint(lambda t, x : B@x, z0, t_gt)
    plot_results(metrics, B, z_pred, z_gt, t_gt, title='Approach 5 — Diagonal log regression')

title: Learning koopman eigenfunctions
text:
Learning koopman eigenfunctions
Here we get to the real deal ! Let’s say we have a set of trajectory points which we don’t know anything about except that they come from the same dynamical system and we want to learn to do inference for a new start point ! We could do auto-regressive models for instance but we want it to be fast for long term inference. In this setup we suppose that the points we have represent the “full state”, they are not noisy or incomplete information and they determine uniquely the future.
Unknown equation : \[
\frac{dx}{dt} = f(x)
\] Data :
\([(x_{k, t_1},  t_1), (x_{k, t_2},  t_2) \cdots (x_{k, t_I}, t_I)]\) for \(k\) trajectories (different initial states)
The times \(t_i\) are not uniformally sampled.
Before starting let’s remember what we learned in the previous notebooks working on simple case-studies :

Normally the reconstruction should be linear function of koopman eigenfunctions (which can be non-linear function of the data)
If we multiply several koopman eigenfunctions together we obtain a new one
Koopman eigenfunctions evolve independently of each other, in parallel
They can be complex and we need complex eigenfunctions to represent rotations
Often koopman eigenfunctions and eigenvalues depend on the parameters of the dynamic so if they change in the dataset we need to take that in account
We don’t necessarly needs to evaluate the reconstruction ability on trajectory points only : it should be true for any valid point that the dynamic could output
\(g(x)\) doesn’t have to be identity, we could train a koopman network for any function of \(x\).

The objective of learning a koopman eigenfunctions is :
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \{\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{D}\} = \arg\min_{\mathcal{E},\, \mathcal{D}} \; &\mathbb{E}_{x \sim \rho}\Big[ \big\| g(x) - \mathcal{D}\big(\mathcal{E}(x)\big) \big\|^2 \Big] \\
  \text{s.t.}\quad &\exists\, A \;:\; \mathcal{E}\big(T(x,\Delta t)\big) = e^{A \Delta t}\,\mathcal{E}(x) \quad \text{for } \rho\text{-almost every } x
  \end{aligned}
\] We take \(\rho\) to be the distribution of states reachable by the dynamic: sampling an initial condition \(x_0 \sim p_0\) and a time \(t \sim p_T\). It is the density of “realistic states”.
Although this objective is hard to reach, especially the constraint part. Looking at the existing deep learning methods there is two common way to adress it (DMD don’t work too well on those data as the \(t\) are not equally spaced and could be far appart) :

Unrolling : latent dynamic linear by construction

\[
\min_{A, \mathcal E, \mathcal D} ||x_{t+\Delta_t} - \mathcal D(e^{A \Delta_t}\mathcal E({x_t}))||_2^2
\]
For instance in : “NIGO: Lyapunov-Stable Continuous-Time Neural Operators for Long-Horizon PDE Dynamics”
We can use either the exponential function or a neural ODE technique.

Dual minimisation : lagrange formulation perspective on this \[
\min_{A, \mathcal E, \mathcal D} ||x_{t} - \mathcal D(\mathcal E({x_t}))||_2^2 + \alpha ||\mathcal E(x_{t + \Delta_t}) - e^{A \Delta_t} \mathcal E({x_t})||_2^2
\]

The advantage of that is that it doesn’t require to do the full backprop through the prediction.
For instance in : “Deep learning for universal linear embeddings of nonlinear dynamics”
Note : For those two methods we could make the reconstruction linear choosing a specific \(\mathcal D\) and we could restreint the dynamic to be independent for each latent dymension constraining A.
